statements.label: supported
statements.text: In living C. elegans, RDE-3 attaches pUG tails to RNA interference targets and to transposon RNAs.
statements.evidence: Here we show that, in its natural context in C. elegans, RDE-3 adds pUG tails to targets of RNA interference, as well as to transposon RNAs.
statements.note: The abstract reports that in its natural context RDE-3 adds pUG tails both to RNAi targets and to transposon RNAs.

statements.label: not_addressed
statements.text: Human homologs of RDE-3 also attach pUG tails to transposon RNAs to silence them.
statements.evidence: RDE-3 (also known as MUT-2) is a ribonucleotidyltransferase that is required for transposon silencing and RNA interference in Caenorhabditis elegans
statements.note: The abstract describes RDE-3 only in C. elegans and in heterologous expression systems and says nothing about human homologs.

statements.label: supported
statements.text: In C. elegans, a pUG tail promotes gene silencing by recruiting RNA-dependent RNA polymerases that copy pUG RNAs into small interfering RNAs.
statements.evidence: pUG tails promote gene silencing by recruiting RNA-dependent RNA polymerases, which use pUG-tailed RNAs (pUG RNAs) as templates to synthesize small interfering RNAs (siRNAs).
statements.note: The abstract states that pUG tails promote gene silencing by recruiting RNA-dependent RNA polymerases that use pUG RNAs as templates for siRNA synthesis.

statements.label: supported
statements.text: An RNA fragment becomes a gene-silencing agent when its attached pUG tail has over 16 perfectly alternating U and G nucleotides.
statements.evidence: RNA fragments attached to pUG tails with more than 16 perfectly alternating 3' U and G nucleotides become gene-silencing agents.
statements.note: The abstract gives the threshold: pUG tails with more than 16 perfectly alternating U and G nucleotides make the attached RNA fragment a silencing agent.

statements.label: supported
statements.text: For translation to be switched on, piRNAs must base-pair with target mRNA 3' UTRs and couple with AU-rich elements to assemble a MIWI/piRNA/eIF3f/HuR super-complex.
statements.evidence: Such action requires specific base-pairing interactions of piRNAs with target mRNAs in their 3' UTRs, which activates translation through coupling with cis-acting AU-rich elements to nucleate the formation of a MIWI/piRNA/eIF3f/HuR super-complex in a developmental stage-specific manner.
statements.note: The abstract says the effect requires piRNA base-pairing in target 3' UTRs, coupled with AU-rich elements, to nucleate a MIWI/piRNA/eIF3f/HuR super-complex.

statements.label: supported
statements.text: During the transformation into spermatozoa, the MIWI/piRNA machinery activates translation of selected spermiogenic mRNAs.
statements.evidence: Here we unexpectedly discover that the same machinery is also responsible for activating translation of a subset of spermiogenic mRNAs to coordinate with morphological transformation into spermatozoa.
statements.note: The abstract reports that the MIWI/piRNA machinery is responsible for activating translation of a subset of spermiogenic mRNAs during the transformation into spermatozoa.

statements.label: not_addressed
statements.text: The piRNA-dependent activation of translation seen in spermatids also operates in developing oocytes.
statements.evidence: the same machinery is also responsible for activating translation of a subset of spermiogenic mRNAs
statements.note: The abstract studies only spermiogenesis and says nothing about oocytes, so it neither supports nor rules out this claim.

statements.label: supported
statements.text: The study found that spermatid development depends on the piRNA system's ability to switch on translation.
statements.evidence: These findings reveal a critical role of the piRNA system in translation activation, which we show is functionally required for spermatid development.
statements.note: The abstract states that piRNA-driven translation activation is functionally required for spermatid development.

statements.label: supported
statements.text: A target-centred functional screen paired murine transposable elements with the KRAB-ZFPs that specifically recognise them.
statements.evidence: Using a target-centered functional screen, we matched murine TEs with their cognate KRAB-ZFP.
statements.note: The abstract reports that a target-centered functional screen matched murine TEs with their cognate KRAB-ZFPs.

statements.label: not_addressed
statements.text: ZFP932 and Gm15446 can bind their ERVK targets only when KAP1 is present.
statements.evidence: KRAB-containing zinc finger proteins (KRAB-ZFPs) are early embryonic controllers of transposable elements (TEs), which they repress with their cofactor KAP1 through histone and DNA methylation
statements.note: KAP1 is named as the repression cofactor, but the abstract does not test whether ZFP932 or Gm15446 binding depends on it.

statements.label: supported
statements.text: Beyond early embryogenesis, these KRAB-ZFPs and KAP1 also control transposable elements in adult tissues, both in cell culture and in vivo.
statements.evidence: Most importantly, we uncovered that these KRAB-ZFPs and KAP1 control TEs in adult tissues, in cell culture and in vivo, where they partner up to modulate cellular genes.
statements.note: The abstract reports that these KRAB-ZFPs and KAP1 control TEs in adult tissues, in cell culture and in vivo.

statements.label: supported
statements.text: In embryonic stem cells, the paralogs ZFP932 and Gm15446 bind partly overlapping sets of ERVK elements and keep them repressed.
statements.evidence: We found the paralogs ZFP932 and Gm15446 to bind overlapping but distinguishable subsets of ERVK (endogenous retrovirus K), repress these elements in embryonic stem cells, and regulate secondarily the expression of neighboring genes.
statements.note: The abstract says ZFP932 and Gm15446 bind overlapping but distinguishable ERVK subsets and repress these elements in embryonic stem cells.

statements.label: not_addressed
statements.text: After fertilization, pollen-derived tRFs are delivered to the zygote, where they keep silencing transposable elements.
statements.evidence: The data presented here demonstrate that tRFs are bona-fide regulatory microRNA-like small RNAs involved in the regulation of genome stability through the targeting of TE transcripts.
statements.note: The abstract covers tRF accumulation in pollen and cleavage of TE mRNAs but says nothing about transfer of tRFs to the zygote.

statements.label: supported
statements.text: Once loaded into AGO1, tRFs specifically guide cleavage of mRNAs made by transcriptionally active endogenous transposable elements.
statements.evidence: the tRF-AGO1 complex acts to specifically target and cleave endogenous transposable element (TE) mRNAs produced from transcriptionally active TEs
statements.note: The abstract reports that the tRF-AGO1 complex specifically targets and cleaves TE mRNAs produced from transcriptionally active TEs.

statements.label: supported
statements.text: tRFs are abundant in the pollen of unstressed wild-type flowering plants and in comparable reproductive structures of non-flowering plants.
statements.evidence: We identified that in the unstressed wild-type male gamete containing pollen of flowering plants, and analogous reproductive structure in non-flowering plant species, tRFs accumulate to high levels.
statements.note: The abstract reports that tRFs accumulate to high levels in unstressed wild-type pollen and in analogous structures of non-flowering plants.

statements.label: supported
statements.text: tRFs are small RNAs of 18 to 26 nucleotides cut specifically from mature tRNAs instead of arising as random degradation products.
statements.evidence: tRNA-derived RNA fragments (tRFs) are 18-26 nucleotide small RNAs that are not random degradation products, but are rather specifically cleaved from mature tRNA transcripts.
statements.note: The abstract describes tRFs as 18-26 nucleotide small RNAs specifically cleaved from mature tRNAs, not random degradation products.

statements.label: supported
statements.text: Editing an endogenous target site showed that 3' pairing dictates which miRNA family member acts on it and that seed pairing alone is not always enough.
statements.evidence: By editing an endogenous target site, we demonstrate that 3' pairing determines targeting by specific miRNA family members and that seed pairing is not always sufficient for functional target interactions.
statements.note: The abstract reports that editing an endogenous site showed 3' pairing determines family-member specificity and seed pairing is not always sufficient.

statements.label: not_addressed
statements.text: Chimera PCR (ChimP) detects specific miRNA–target interactions with higher sensitivity than iCLIP.
statements.evidence: Finally, we present a simplified method, chimera PCR (ChimP), for the detection of specific miRNA-target interactions.
statements.note: The abstract presents ChimP as a simplified detection method but does not compare its sensitivity with iCLIP.

statements.label: supported
statements.text: Most miRNA target sites pair with 3' sequences of the miRNA in addition to the seed.
statements.evidence: Unexpectedly, we discovered that additional pairing to 3' sequences is prevalent in the majority of target sites and leads to specific targeting by members of miRNA families.
statements.note: The abstract reports that additional pairing to 3' sequences is prevalent in the majority of target sites.

statements.label: supported
statements.text: Across thousands of reproducible chimeras, pairing to the miRNA seed was the main motif linked to functional interactions.
statements.evidence: Through the analysis of thousands of reproducible chimeras, pairing to the miRNA seed emerged as the predominant motif associated with functional interactions.
statements.note: The abstract reports that analysis of thousands of reproducible chimeras identified seed pairing as the predominant motif of functional interactions.

statements.label: supported
statements.text: Through 3' trimming, the near-perfect miR-29 binding site selectively destabilises miR-29b and confines its spatial expression in the cerebellum.
statements.evidence: We show that the near-perfect miRNA site selectively triggers miR-29b destabilization through 3' trimming and restricts its spatial expression in the cerebellum.
statements.note: The abstract states that the near-perfect site triggers miR-29b destabilization through 3' trimming and restricts its spatial expression in the cerebellum.

statements.label: supported
statements.text: Mice with a disrupted miR-29 site in Nrep showed ectopic miR-29b expression in the cerebellum and worsened coordination and motor learning.
statements.evidence: Genetic disruption of the miR-29 site within mouse Nrep results in ectopic expression of cerebellar miR-29b and impaired coordination and motor learning.
statements.note: The abstract reports that disrupting the miR-29 site in mouse Nrep causes ectopic cerebellar miR-29b and impaired coordination and motor learning.

statements.label: not_addressed
statements.text: People carrying mutations in the miR-29 site of NREP have impaired motor coordination.
statements.evidence: Here, we show that a genome-encoded transcript harboring a near-perfect and deeply conserved miRNA-binding site for miR-29 controls zebrafish and mouse behavior.
statements.note: The behavioural effects are shown only in zebrafish and mice; the abstract says nothing about human carriers of site mutations.

statements.label: supported
statements.text: The transcript carrying the miR-29 site arose in basal vertebrates as a lncRNA and became the protein-coding gene NREP in mammals, with the site in its 3' UTR.
statements.evidence: This transcript originated in basal vertebrates as a long noncoding RNA (lncRNA) and evolved to the protein-coding gene NREP in mammals, where the miR-29-binding site is located within the 3' UTR.
statements.note: The abstract traces the transcript from a basal-vertebrate lncRNA to the mammalian protein-coding gene NREP, whose 3' UTR holds the miR-29 site.

statements.label: supported
statements.text: Mature microRNAs are generated within minutes, reflecting tightly coupled biogenesis that uridylation of pre-miRNAs selectively disrupts.
statements.evidence: Mature microRNAs are produced within minutes, revealing tight intracellular coupling of biogenesis that is selectively disrupted by pre-miRNA-uridylation.
statements.note: The abstract reports that mature microRNAs are produced within minutes and that pre-miRNA uridylation selectively disrupts this tight coupling.

statements.label: supported
statements.text: In Drosophila cells, microRNAs are among the quickest-made and longest-lived transcripts, reaching up to 10^5 copies per cell at steady state.
statements.evidence: Based on absolute rate of biogenesis and decay, microRNAs rank among the fastest produced and longest-lived cellular transcripts, disposing up to 10 5 copies per cell at steady-state.
statements.note: The abstract ranks microRNAs among the fastest produced and longest-lived cellular transcripts, with up to 10^5 copies per cell at steady state.

statements.label: supported
statements.text: Regulated small RNA decay turns over Ago1-bound microRNAs faster than Ago2-bound small interfering RNAs.
statements.evidence: Finally, regulated small RNA decay enables the selective rapid turnover of Ago1-bound microRNAs, but not of Ago2-bound small interfering RNAs (siRNAs), reflecting key differences in the robustness of small RNA silencing pathways.
statements.note: The abstract says regulated decay enables selective rapid turnover of Ago1-bound microRNAs but not of Ago2-bound siRNAs.

statements.label: not_addressed
statements.text: MicroRNAs in mammalian cells are produced as quickly and persist as long as those measured in Drosophila.
statements.evidence: We employed metabolic small RNA sequencing for a comprehensive view on intracellular microRNA kinetics in Drosophila.
statements.note: The kinetics were measured only in Drosophila; the abstract makes no comparison with mammalian cells.

statements.label: supported
statements.text: Either the male or the female germline can pass learned PA14 avoidance to C. elegans progeny, and the behaviour persists into the fourth generation.
statements.evidence: We discovered that, after C. elegans have learned to avoid the pathogenic bacteria Pseudomonas aeruginosa (PA14), they pass this learned behavior on to their progeny, through either the male or female germline, persisting through the fourth generation.
statements.note: The abstract reports that learned PA14 avoidance passes to progeny through either germline and persists through the fourth generation.

statements.label: not_addressed
statements.text: Learned avoidance of other pathogenic bacteria, such as Serratia marcescens, is likewise inherited by C. elegans progeny.
statements.evidence: after C. elegans have learned to avoid the pathogenic bacteria Pseudomonas aeruginosa (PA14), they pass this learned behavior on to their progeny
statements.note: The abstract tests only Pseudomonas aeruginosa PA14 and says nothing about other pathogens.

statements.label: supported
statements.text: Expression of the TGF-β ligand DAF-7 in ASI sensory neurons tracks with the inherited avoidance behaviour and is needed for it.
statements.evidence: Expression of the TGF-β ligand DAF-7 in the ASI sensory neurons correlates with and is required for this transgenerational avoidance behavior.
statements.note: The abstract states that DAF-7 expression in ASI neurons correlates with and is required for the transgenerational avoidance behavior.

statements.label: supported
statements.text: Progeny of parents that learned to avoid PA14 had higher survival owing to PA14 avoidance, and this effect depended on prg-1.
statements.evidence: Animals whose parents have learned to avoid PA14 display a PA14 avoidance-based survival advantage that is also prg-1 dependent, suggesting an adaptive response.
statements.note: The abstract reports a PA14 avoidance-based survival advantage in progeny of trained parents that is prg-1 dependent.

statements.label: not_addressed
statements.text: P11 RNA travels from the worm's intestine to the ASI neuron to trigger avoidance of PA14.
statements.evidence: The RNA interference (RNAi) and PIWI-interacting RNA (piRNA) pathways, the germline and the ASI neuron are all required for avoidance behaviour induced by bacterial small RNAs
statements.note: The abstract says the ASI neuron is required but does not describe how P11 reaches it or which tissues it passes through.

statements.label: supported
statements.text: Avoidance triggered by bacterial small RNAs, and its inheritance across generations, needs the RNAi and piRNA pathways, the germline and the ASI neuron.
statements.evidence: The RNA interference (RNAi) and PIWI-interacting RNA (piRNA) pathways, the germline and the ASI neuron are all required for avoidance behaviour induced by bacterial small RNAs, and for the transgenerational inheritance of this behaviour.
statements.note: The abstract states that the RNAi and piRNA pathways, the germline and the ASI neuron are all required for the behaviour and its inheritance.

statements.label: supported
statements.text: P11, a single non-coding RNA of P. aeruginosa, is required and sufficient for learned PA14 avoidance, which also needs the worm gene it targets, maco-1.
statements.evidence: A single P. aeruginosa non-coding RNA, P11, is both necessary and sufficient to convey learned avoidance of PA14, and its C. elegans target, maco-1, is required for avoidance.
statements.note: The abstract reports that P11 is necessary and sufficient to convey learned PA14 avoidance and that its C. elegans target maco-1 is required.

statements.label: supported
statements.text: One exposure to purified PA14 small RNAs was enough to increase pathogen avoidance in treated worms and in the next four generations of their progeny.
statements.evidence: Here we show that a single exposure to purified small RNAs isolated from pathogenic Pseudomonas aeruginosa (PA14) is sufficient to induce pathogen avoidance in the treated worms and in four subsequent generations of progeny.
statements.note: The abstract states that a single exposure to purified PA14 small RNAs induces pathogen avoidance in treated worms and four subsequent generations.

statements.label: supported
statements.text: Small RNAs synthesised only in neurons, in an RDE-4-dependent way, regulate amplified endogenous siRNAs and gene expression in the germline over several generations.
statements.evidence: Neurons-specific synthesis of RDE-4-dependent small RNAs regulates germline amplified endogenous small interfering RNAs (siRNAs) and germline gene expression for multiple generations.
statements.note: The abstract reports that neuron-specific RDE-4-dependent small RNAs regulate germline amplified endogenous siRNAs and germline gene expression for multiple generations.

statements.label: not_addressed
statements.text: Small RNAs made in neurons reach the germline packaged inside extracellular vesicles.
statements.evidence: Thus, we propose a small-RNA-based mechanism for communication of neuronal processes transgenerationally.
statements.note: The abstract proposes a small-RNA-based mechanism but does not say how neuronal small RNAs reach the germline.

statements.label: supported
statements.text: The gene saeg-2, a target of neuronal small RNAs, is downregulated in the germline across generations.
statements.evidence: Among the targets of these small RNAs, we identified the conserved gene saeg-2, which is transgenerationally downregulated in the germline.
statements.note: The abstract identifies saeg-2 as a target of these small RNAs that is transgenerationally downregulated in the germline.

statements.label: supported
statements.text: Via the germline Argonaute HRDE-1, small RNAs produced in neurons control the chemotaxis behaviour of progeny for no less than three generations.
statements.evidence: Further, the production of small RNAs in neurons controls the chemotaxis behavior of the progeny for at least three generations via the germline Argonaute HRDE-1.
statements.note: The abstract reports that neuronal small RNA production controls progeny chemotaxis for at least three generations via the germline Argonaute HRDE-1.
